This was highly unsettling, one of biggest fears. Well done.

So all those nature documentaries always say shark attacks are usually a case of a shark mistaking a person for a fish. I guess I kinda feel like that doesn't take into account unforeseen factors like how hungry the shark is and whether or not the person has a bleeding cut or something but just for the sake of argument: I feel like paddling away like he did would make him seem more like a fish, would it not? What would happen if he were to stick his face in the water and let out a blood curdling high pitched screech as loud as he could? Would that confuse the shark? I feel like that's not something most of the shark's prey would have ever done before and might make the shark weirded out enough to leave. Wait can sharks even hear? I'm just saying that being very quiet and paddling away hurriedly seems like exactly the behavior of prey...

I'm not a biologist by any means but from what I learned in school all animals live to fulfill two purposes: survive and reproduce. When it comes to interacting with the unfamiliar (a dude on a surfboard) the shark can take 1 of 3 options: Investigate, fight, or flight. An apex predator like a white shark isn't going to flee from most scenarios, which leaves the first two options. If he wanted to make a meal of this guy he certainly could have but something in its brain was telling it that this isn't a typical meal-it doesn't behave like a typical meal, and its senses arent telling the shark it's a typical meal.

I know we humans like to make the analogy that a guy on a surfboard looks like a seal and that's why surfers get attacked. This is sort of far-fetched. Have you ever seen a seal swimming? It looks nothing like a surfer. They're fast, they jump, they dart left and right and up and down. I suppose for a moment, when viewed from directly underneath, the outline may resemble something like a seal, but beyond that there aren't many similarities. Seals have a scent that can be detected by white sharks. Their movements are familiar to white sharks. This guy, other than briefly resembling the outline, isn't tripping any of the shark's alarms that "hey, this is totally a seal. Better gobble him up". Even him paddling away doesn't resemble prey behavior. Even if it was frantic from our human perspective the shark has no frame of reference to a long skinny thing with two army dangly things propelling it forward. I'm 99.999% confident the shark was simply curious about the surfer and wanted to simply check him out.

As for why people get attacked by white sharks occasionally there's two reasons: one is to investigate. Sharks dont have fingers and arms. They can't talk. They use what they have-their mouths, to receive information when determining whether something is worth the effort of a meal. This is often why white shark victims lose a limb, the shark takes a bite (albeit a very large one), determines that we're far too lean and boney to consume and moves on. Unfortunately for us that bite can often be fatal. The second reason is one you alluded to-the shark could be desperate. Maybe it's been weeks since its last meal and at this point it needs food, doesnt care what it is. These are the very rare instances when a human is truly consumed by a white shark. I haven't seen the statistics in a long time but I know there's only a handful of reported cases of humans being fully consumed by white sharks. White sharks didn't evolve to consume us and we aren't their natural prey. There's much meatier stuff swimming in the ocean for Jaws to chomp down on. If life's gotten so tough for a shark that we suddenly become appetizing the shark likely isn't doing very well.

Hope this explains things. Feel free to respond and I'll try to expand some more on some of the details.

I'm still curious about possible methods to deter the shark. I guess my question is what's the course of action the surfer should have taken to most discourage the shark from taking a bite? Did he do the right thing by paddling away because my instinct would be that that would be a bad idea because in my mind it gives off the same signals as the shark's other prey sorta. Obviously it worked out since the shark didn't do anything but I cant help but wonder what would happen if the surfer was just still and not making any sound until maybe the shark got bored and moved on. Or better yet, how would the shark react to an aggressive behavior like screaming in the water? Maybe screaming or being still would make it more likely to attack?

In my opinion, if it were me, I'd have done the exact same thing. A great white is an apex predator and can rip you in two with one bite. Whether the shark meant to take that bite because it was hungry or because it was curious doesn't matter to me-I'd be dead. You can't really do much to deter a shark, screaming something underwater may help because our screams have to be foreign to them and unrecognizable. However, to the best of my knowledge sharks mostly sense through their nose and I'm not familiar with how their hearing has evolved. Sharks can certainly understand distress so splashing around may either frighten the shark (because our splashing wouldn't be a completely understood action) or tell the shark we are in trouble and an easy target.

Your best bet if you're ever in a scenario like this is to try your damnedest to remain calm and get to shore as fast as possible. Remember the shark is curious about you, but not in a "want to get to know you better" kind of way. He's curious as to whether you're worth consuming.
